context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.1; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: A Helper at Home: Promise and Practical Questions
body: A proposed care scheme would give older public-housing tenants who live alone financial help to employ a domestic helper. Supporters say daily assistance could allow more people to remain in familiar neighbourhoods instead of entering residential homes. A helper might prepare meals, keep the flat clean, collect medicine and notice quickly when an elderly person becomes unwell.

The arrangement is not as simple as paying a salary. Some tenants may struggle to interview workers, complete paperwork or communicate across a language barrier. Sharing a very small flat can reduce privacy for both people. Families also want safeguards against neglect, financial abuse and sudden contract disputes, while helpers need reasonable hours, training and somewhere suitable to sleep.

Community nurses, meal deliveries, emergency alarms and regular visits from social workers could support those who do not want a live-in helper. Neighbourhood volunteers may reduce loneliness, but they cannot replace professional care. Before launching the scheme widely, officials should ask elderly residents what they prefer and explain who will monitor each placement when problems arise.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.2; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: Can Hong Kong’s Leading Broadcaster Win Viewers Back?
body: For decades, families planned their evenings around the same television dramas, variety shows and news bulletins. TVB stars became household names, and popular series gave people common jokes and stories to discuss at school or work. That shared audience made the station an important part of local entertainment and helped advertisers reach almost every age group.

Viewing habits have changed sharply. Young people can stream Korean, mainland Chinese, Western and independent local programmes whenever they choose. Some former fans complain that familiar plots, repeated locations and a small circle of actors make new dramas feel predictable. Online platforms also release complete seasons at once, while traditional schedules require viewers to wait for the next episode.

The broadcaster still owns a valuable archive and understands Cantonese audiences. A recovery might depend on investing in new writers, giving unfamiliar performers a chance and producing stories that reflect present-day Hong Kong. Short online editions, reliable subtitles and legal international streaming could reach viewers beyond free-to-air television. Success will require more than nostalgia; audiences must feel that the programmes deserve their time again.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: When School Messages Follow Teachers Home
body: Class messaging groups make it easy to announce a timetable change, share a missing worksheet or check whether a student arrived safely. Parents appreciate receiving information quickly, and shy students sometimes find it easier to type a short question than approach a teacher in a crowded corridor. During an emergency, instant contact can prevent confusion.

Problems begin when every message is treated as urgent. A teacher may receive homework questions late at night, repeated reminders from parents and complaints that have already been answered. Group chats can expose phone numbers, spread rumours or embarrass a student in front of the whole class. Fast replies may also create an expectation that staff are permanently on duty.

One school is considering a single official platform with weekday contact hours. Teachers would answer routine questions on the next working day, while genuine safety matters would go through an emergency channel. Sensitive concerns would move to a private meeting rather than remain in a chat. Clear rules for students, parents and staff could preserve the convenience of messaging without allowing it to replace respectful face-to-face communication.

context.title: A Bike When You Need One
body: A new operator plans to place app-activated bicycles near housing estates, railway stations and cycle tracks. Riders would unlock a bicycle for a small fee, use it for a short journey and leave it at an approved parking area. The company believes the service can solve the awkward “last kilometre” between public transport and home.

Shared bicycles could reduce car journeys, provide inexpensive exercise and help residents who have no room to store a bike. Yet early trials have produced familiar complaints: damaged bicycles, blocked pavements, careless parking and riders entering busy roads without helmets. Users may also worry about deposits, personal data and whether a broken bicycle will be repaired promptly.

District councils could mark parking bays, expand safe cycling routes and fine operators that fail to remove abandoned bikes. The app should report faults and prevent new rentals from unsafe locations. If the model works, other neighbourhood schemes might lend umbrellas, tools, sports equipment or small vehicles. Each service would still need clear responsibility for maintenance, insurance and fair access.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.2; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: A Welcome Camp for New S1 Students
body: The student council has proposed a two-day orientation camp before the new school term. Small mixed teams would explore the campus, meet senior student leaders and complete simple challenges together. Organisers hope newcomers will recognise friendly faces on their first morning and feel more confident asking for help.

A camp can build belonging, but compulsory cheering, late-night games or public performances may frighten quieter students. Fees could exclude some families, and children with disabilities, food allergies or religious needs may require adjustments. Anyone unable to attend should not begin the year feeling that every friendship group has already formed without them.

Suggested activities include a photo-free campus trail, a cooperative puzzle, a club fair and a relaxed picnic with form teachers. Students could choose between energetic and quiet sessions instead of being forced onto a stage. The school would need consent forms, trained leaders, first-aid cover, transport arrangements and a bad-weather plan. A follow-up lunch in the first week could welcome absentees and help staff check whether the camp achieved its purpose.

context.title: Cash Support for Students Facing a Major Examination
body: A charitable foundation is testing a grant for secondary students preparing for a public examination. The money would be paid directly to candidates in selected districts, without requiring receipts. The foundation says young people should decide whether they most need transport, meals, revision books, internet access or a quieter place to study.

Teachers welcome help for families under pressure, but opinions differ about an unconditional payment. Some students may use it carefully, while others could spend it on entertainment or expensive gadgets. Limiting the first round to a few districts is easy to administer, yet candidates with similar financial difficulties elsewhere may see the arrangement as unfair.

The pilot could include a short, optional money-management workshop and confidential advice for students facing debt at home. After the examination, anonymous surveys could show which expenses mattered most without policing every purchase. If the programme expands, the foundation must choose between a universal grant and support based on household need. That decision will affect cost, dignity, paperwork and whether help reaches students who might otherwise be overlooked.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice with 2018 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.1; this is not HKEAA text:
context.title: Why an Empty Hour May Not Be Wasted
body: Many teenagers move directly from lessons to tutorials, music practice, sport and homework. Parents often arrange these activities with good intentions, believing that every hour should develop a useful skill. A school counsellor, however, has suggested that students also need unplanned time in which nobody sets a target or measures their performance.

Quiet periods can allow the mind to wander, recover from stress and connect ideas in unexpected ways. A bored student may begin drawing, reading, repairing something or simply thinking through a difficult day. Doing nothing is not automatically healthy: endless scrolling, avoiding responsibilities or staying isolated for long periods can leave a young person more tired than before.

The school could trial one homework-light evening and ask families to observe the effect on sleep, mood and creativity. Students would be free to rest or choose their own activity, preferably away from constant notifications. Explaining the experiment to parents with evidence and student reflections may be more convincing than telling them to abandon structure. The aim is balance, not laziness.

body: A well-known music producer recently complained that young performers lack patience and expect success after a single online video. Similar comments accuse teenagers of avoiding hard work, depending on parents and caring more about phones than real skills. Older listeners recognise the frustration, especially when they remember long apprenticeships and fewer shortcuts to publicity.

The criticism misses part of the picture. Young people face intense examinations, high housing costs and a job market in which technology can remove familiar careers. Adults can help by offering practical mentoring, paid entry-level opportunities and honest accounts of failure. Teenagers, in return, should accept that talent still needs practice and reliability. A useful conversation begins when both generations replace stereotypes with specific examples.

Greater freedom may help students balancing part-time work, illness or family duties. Millions watched her performance, while viewers argued about whether a child should face such public attention. Competitions can build confidence, provide professional feedback and open doors that ordinary lessons cannot. Children may learn to practise consistently and recover from disappointment. Promotion should target local neighbourhoods as well as tourists.
